# Bandhanāgārajātaka (Ja 201)

**ID:** Ja 201
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Bandhanāgārajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bandhanāgārajātaka* (Ja 201; PTS Ja II 56–57) is a narrative found in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [Catalog; Fausböll 1879; von Hinüber 1996]. The Buddha delivers the discourse while residing at Jetavana concerning a prison-house (*bandhanāgāra*), after seeing thieves bound in cords, ropes, and chains by the king of Kosala [Fausböll 1879]. Its core verse opens with *Na taṁ daḷhaṁ bandhanam āhu dhīrā* ("Wise men say that is not a strong fetter"), emphasizing that material fetters made of iron, wood, or rope are insignificant compared to the binding attachment to jewelry, wealth, wives, and children [Fausböll 1879; Fenn 1994]. In the narrative, the Bodhisattva abandons his pregnant wife and child to seek ascetic ordination, illustrating a radical renunciation of domestic ties construed as bonds of craving [Fenn 1994; Fausböll 1879].

 DharmaNexus confirms substantial text reuse with Dhp, SN 3, the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2), and the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 9, Ne 37), in addition to cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit Patna Dharmapada, the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (D4099), and the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali literature, story 85 of the Chinese *Liudu jijing* has also been identified as an adaptation of the *Bandhanāgāra* narrative [Huynh 2016].

Scholars have noted that although the verses and story line in the Jātaka correspond closely to the narrative in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, the verse commentaries diverge markedly [Burlingame 1921; von Hinüber 1996]. Oskar von Hinüber observes that this divergence in the exegesis of identical verses reflects distinct, independent reciter traditions preserved by the *jātaka-bhāṇakas* and *dhammapada-bhāṇakas* [von Hinüber 1996].
